positions/christian-sabbath-sabbatarian/: Christian Sabbath (first-day Sabbatarianism)
Puritan Sabbath
Lord’s Day Sabbatarianism
Westminster view of the Lord’s Day

The fourth commandment is a perpetual moral law grounded in creation; since Christ’s resurrection the Sabbath has been transferred to the first day, which should be kept wholly for worship, rest and works of necessity and mercy.
The Sabbath was instituted at creation (Gen 2:2–3) before Moses, so it is not merely ceremonial.
The fourth commandment stands among the moral Ten Commandments.
The resurrection moved the day to the first day of the week, "the Lord’s Day" (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10).
The whole day is to be devoted to public and private worship, rest from ordinary work and recreations, and mercy (WCF 21.8).
Genesis 2:2–3
Exodus 20:8–11
Isaiah 58:13–14
Hebrews 4:9
Westminster Confession 21.7–8

Developed in English Puritanism (Nicholas Bownde, The Doctrine of the Sabbath, 1595) amid controversy over James I’s Book of Sports (1618, reissued 1633); codified by the Westminster Assembly (1647) and expounded by John Owen (Exercitations on the Lord’s Day, 1671). It shaped Scottish, Welsh, New England and later Korean and Pacific Islander Protestant culture.
Nicholas Bownde
Lancelot Andrewes (moderate)
Robert Murray M’Cheyne
Joseph Pipa
Free Church of Scotland
Its roots in creation and placement in the Decalogue suggest permanence.
Hebrews 4:9 says "there remaineth therefore a rest (sabbatismos) to the people of God".
The early church’s shift to the first day is best explained as apostolic practice reflecting the resurrection.
No New Testament text explicitly transfers the Sabbath command to Sunday; Paul treats days as matters of conscience (Rom 14:5; Col 2:16).
Seventh-day keepers object that if the commandment is moral and perpetual, its specified day should be too.
Many Christians (Lutherans, Calvin himself, Catholics) regard strict Sabbatarianism as a legalism the Reformers did not hold.
Sabbatarians reply that the principle of one day in seven is moral while the specific day is determined by redemptive history, as the resurrection shows.
They read Colossians 2:16 as referring to Jewish ceremonial sabbaths, not the creation ordinance.
"Blue laws" and Sunday closing in Britain, North America and elsewhere.
Campaigns against Sunday trading, sport and mail delivery (19th–20th centuries).
Persistent Sunday observance cultures in Scotland’s Hebrides, Korea, Tonga and Samoa.
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/name: The Lord’s Day as Christian festival (non-Sabbatarian)
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/oneL: The seventh-day Sabbath was a sign for Israel fulfilled in Christ’s rest; Christians gather on the first day, the day of resurrection, by apostolic custom and church order, keeping it joyfully without imposing Jewish Sabbath rules.
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/core: The Sabbath command’s ceremonial aspect is fulfilled in Christ, who gives rest to the weary (Matt 11:28; Heb 4).
The Lord’s Day is the "eighth day" of new creation, celebrated with the Eucharist since apostolic times.
The church may appoint the day and rules for its observance; Catholics are obliged to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days (CCC 2180–2185).
Rest and worship remain good, but strict prohibitions are not binding law.
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/orig: The early church worshipped on Sunday from at least c.110 (Ignatius; Pliny’s letter c.112; Justin, First Apology 67, c.155); Constantine made Sunday a civil day of rest (321). Aquinas treated the Sabbath command as partly moral, partly ceremonial; Luther (Large Catechism, 1529) and Calvin (Institutes 2.8.28–34) rejected Sabbatarian legalism.
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/stro: Paul classes Sabbaths with festivals and new moons as "a shadow of things to come" (Col 2:16–17).
The earliest post-apostolic witnesses consistently describe a Sunday gathering, not a transferred Sabbath.
It honours Jesus’ teaching that "the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27).
Sabbatarians argue it weakens a creation ordinance and leads to secularised Sundays.
Seventh-day keepers argue that the change of day lacks biblical warrant and reflects later church authority.
Some critics see Catholic Sunday obligation as itself a new legal rule.
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/resp: Advocates answer that the Lord’s Day is kept out of love and the need for common worship, and that weakening of observance stems from culture, not theology.
They point to the pre-Constantinian evidence (Ignatius, Didache 14, Justin) to show that Sunday worship was apostolic, not imperial or papal.
positions/lords-day-non-sabbatarian/cons: Sunday as the near-universal Christian day of worship.
Catholic and Orthodox structuring of the week around the Sunday Eucharist.
Modern relaxations of Sunday laws accepted by most churches.
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/oneLine: The fourth commandment still requires Christians to rest and worship on the seventh day (Friday sunset to Saturday sunset); the change to Sunday was a later human tradition.
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/coreClaims: The Sabbath is a creation ordinance blessed by God for all humanity (Gen 2:2–3; Mark 2:27).
Jesus and the apostles kept the seventh-day Sabbath; no text authorises a change of day.
The Decalogue is the eternal moral law, written by God’s finger, and the Sabbath is at its centre.
For Seventh-day Adventists the Sabbath will be a final test of loyalty to God (Rev 14:12).
Some Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox practice honours both the seventh day and Sunday.
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/origin: Seventh-day observance continued among some early Christians alongside Sunday (Apostolic Constitutions 7.23) and in Ethiopia, where Emperor Zara Yaqob’s council (c.1450) upheld Saturday observance alongside Sunday; in Protestantism among Seventh Day Baptists in England (1650s) and Rhode Island (1671); adopted by Sabbatarian Adventists after 1846 (Joseph Bates; Ellen G. White) and the Seventh-day Adventist Church (1863); also Church of God (Seventh Day) and some Messianic congregations.
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/strongestA: The text of the commandment specifies "the seventh day"; changing the day changes the commandment.
The New Testament repeatedly records Jesus and Paul in synagogue "on the sabbath day" (Luke 4:16; Acts 17:2).
Sunday worship became fixed in part through anti-Jewish polemic and imperial law (Bacchiocchi).
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/strongestO: Paul declares that no one should judge Christians regarding Sabbath days (Col 2:16) and treats days as matters of conscience (Rom 14:5).
The earliest Christian sources (Ignatius, Didache, Justin) show first-day assembly within decades of the apostles.
Critics argue the Adventist teaching on the Sabbath as eschatological test risks legalism and judgement of other Christians.
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/responses/: Sabbath-keepers reply that Colossians 2:16 addresses ceremonial sabbaths and that early Sunday gatherings did not abolish the seventh-day rest.
Adventists stress that the Sabbath is a gift of grace and sign of creation and redemption, not a means of salvation.
positions/seventh-day-sabbath/consequenc: Defining practice of more than 20 million Seventh-day Adventists worldwide.
Legal cases on Sabbath accommodation in employment and education.
Adventist health and education institutions built around the Sabbath rhythm.
positions/tithing/name: Tithing as a binding Christian obligation
positions/tithing/oneLine: Christians should give a tenth of their income to God through the church, a practice that predates Moses (Abraham, Jacob), was commended by Jesus and is the baseline of faithful stewardship.
positions/tithing/coreClaims/0: Abraham’s tithe to Melchizedek (Gen 14:20) and Jacob’s vow (Gen 28:22) precede the Law, so tithing is not merely Mosaic.
positions/tithing/coreClaims/1: Malachi 3:8–10 calls withholding tithes robbing God and promises blessing to faithful givers.
positions/tithing/coreClaims/2: Jesus affirmed tithing: "these ought ye to have done" (Matt 23:23).
positions/tithing/coreClaims/3: The tithe belongs to the local church ("storehouse"); offerings are given beyond it.
positions/tithing/origin: Some early writers urged Christians to exceed the tithe (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.18); the Second Council of Mâcon (585) and Charlemagne (779) made tithes compulsory church law in the West. Abolished or commuted in modern Europe (France 1789; England, Tithe Commutation Act 1836), the voluntary tithe was revived among 19th–20th-century evangelicals, Adventists, Latter-day Saints (revelation of 1838) and Pentecostals.
positions/tithing/proponentsOther/2: R. T. Kendall (The Gift of Giving)
positions/tithing/proponentsOther/3: many Pentecostal and African independent churches
positions/tithing/strongestArguments/0: The pre-Mosaic examples show the tithe as an enduring pattern of honouring God.
positions/tithing/strongestArguments/1: A clear baseline guards against vague generosity that in practice becomes minimal.
positions/tithing/strongestArguments/2: Churches and missions depend on regular giving; many testify to blessing through faithful tithing.
positions/tithing/strongestObjections/0: The New Testament never commands Christians to tithe; Paul’s collection teaching (2 Cor 8–9) stresses freedom and cheerfulness, "not of necessity".
positions/tithing/strongestObjections/1: Israel’s tithes funded the Levitical system and festivals and were agricultural; transferring them to modern income is inconsistent.
positions/tithing/strongestObjections/2: Prosperity teaching that promises financial return for tithing can exploit the poor (a criticism made by Lausanne’s Cape Town Commitment, 2010).
positions/tithing/responses/0: Tithing advocates reply that the New Testament standard of generosity is higher, not lower, and that the tithe is a sensible starting point.
positions/tithing/responses/1: Many teach tithing as a voluntary covenant of gratitude, not a condition of salvation, and reject manipulative "seed-faith" forms.
positions/tithing/consequences/0: Medieval tithe barns, disputes and anticlerical revolts; abolition in revolutionary France.
positions/tithing/consequences/1: Major funding model for evangelical, Adventist, LDS and Pentecostal churches today.
positions/tithing/consequences/2: State church taxes (e.g. German Kirchensteuer) as a modern successor in some countries.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/name: Creation out of nothing (creatio ex nihilo)
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/oneLine: The one God freely brought into being everything other than himself — matter, time, angels and humans — without any pre-existing material, and sustains it moment by moment.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/coreClaims/0: God alone is eternal and uncreated; everything else has a beginning and depends on him.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/coreClaims/1: Creation is a free act of love, not a necessity or an emanation from God’s being.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/coreClaims/2: Matter is good, not evil or a rival principle.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/coreClaims/3: Creation includes time itself, so God did not “wait” before creating.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/coreClaims/4: The Creator–creature distinction is fundamental to Christian worship and ethics.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/origin: Implicit in Jewish texts (2 Maccabees 7:28) and the New Testament; made explicit against Platonism and Gnosticism by Theophilus of Antioch, Irenaeus and Tertullian (c.180-205); defined by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and Vatican I (1870).
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/proponentsOt: Hermas, Mandate 1 (“who made all things to be out of what was not”)
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/strongestArg: Only creation from nothing preserves God’s absolute sovereignty and uniqueness: nothing exists alongside him independently.
It grounds the goodness of matter against dualism, and so the goodness of body, sex, food and sacraments.
It fits the biblical picture of God calling into existence “the things that are not” and is presupposed by the hope of resurrection.
Many see consonance with big-bang cosmology’s absolute beginning, though the doctrine does not depend on it.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/strongestObj: Process thinkers argue that creation from chaos (Genesis 1:2) is the more natural reading and that ex nihilo creation makes God responsible for all evil.
Historians note that Genesis 1 and much of the Old Testament may describe ordering of chaos rather than absolute origination, so the doctrine is a later inference.
Mormon theology holds that matter (and intelligences) are eternal, and that ex nihilo is a Hellenistic accretion.
Some argue that a timeless God creating time is incoherent.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/responses/0: Defenders reply that the doctrine is a legitimate inference from the whole biblical witness (God as sole source of all things), even if Genesis 1 does not state it in philosophical terms.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/responses/1: On evil: creation from nothing makes creatures finite and mutable, not evil; evil arises from the misuse of freedom (Augustine) or is permitted for greater goods.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/responses/2: Augustine and Aquinas answer the time objection: time is a feature of creation, so “before creation” has no meaning.
positions/creatio-ex-nihilo/consequences: Shaped the Creator–creature distinction that underlies classical theism and the doctrine of grace.
Gave a theological rationale for regarding nature as contingent and orderly — a theme in histories of early modern science.
Separates historic Christianity from Gnostic, Platonist, process and Latter-day Saint cosmologies.
